contentSummary: Binary form is one of the simplest and most common musical forms, used in a wide range of musical styles and genres. It is a fundamental concept in music theory, and understanding binary form helps one analyse and appreciate the structure of many musical compositions. Binary form consists of two contrasting sections, often labeled as A and B. The A section typically presents a theme or melody, while the B section presents a contrasting theme or develops the initial theme. The two sections are usually of equal or approximately equal length.Ternary form on the other hand, is a musical structure consisting of three main sections, typically represented as A-B-A. This means the piece begins with an initial theme or section (A), followed by a contrasting middle section (B), and concludes with a return to the initial theme or section (A). Ternary form provides a sense of balance and symmetry, making it a popular choice for composers and songwriters.Example of Binary form Ternary Form ABA

contentSummary: Most musical terms are written in Italian Language because of the country’s significant contributions to the development of Western classical music. Italian composers were the first to write ‘instruction’ words at certain points in their music. Italian musical terms have become an integral part of the language of music, providing a universal vocabulary for musicians to communicate and interpret music accurately.The term ‘tempo’ is derived from the Italian language. In Italian, ‘tempo’ means ‘time’ and in music, it refers to the speed or rate at which a piece of music is performed.

contentSummary: Musical signs also known as musical notation symbols, are graphical representations used to convey musical information. They help musicians read and interpret musical score. In music, Harmony refers to the combination of different musical notes played or sung at the same time to produce a pleasing sound. It usually supports the melody (the tune) and adds depth, emotion and texture to a piece of music.Harmony is created when two or more notes sound together, forming chords (like C major or G minor), or more complex structures. For instance, if someone sings or plays a melody and another person sings or plays a different note that blends well with it, they are singing or playing in harmony. So when we think of Harmony, we are thinking of layers of sound. It is a fundamental aspect of music, enhancing the emotional impact and aesthetic appeal of a composition. General Competences:Analytical thinking: Ability to systematically examine, interpret and evaluate musical elements and structures, for the purpose of applying them in social-economic needs.Collaboration: Ability to work effectively with others in various musical settings such as ensembles or bands and other music projects to achieve goals in Musical Arts Education.Creativity and Innovation: Ability to experiment new approaches and generate musical ideas that exhibit originality and take risks in the composition, performance and interpretation of music.Critical thinking: Ability to analyse, investigate and evaluate musical works, performances and practices with a discerning and reflective mindset to address social-economical needs.Digital Literacy: Ability to effectively use hardware and software to analyse, create, produce, and share music.Problem solving: Ability to use music to identify, analyse and address social-economical challenges and obstacles.TERMINOLOGYCadence: A chord progression that signals the end of a phrase or section. (perfect cadence (V-I).Chord: Is formed when two or more different notes are played or sung together. The most common is a Triad, which consists of 3 notes (C-E-G).Chord progression: Is a sequence of chords played in successions. (I - IV - V - I)Consonance: A combination of notes that sounds stable, pleasant or resolved.Dissonance: A combination of notes that sounds tense or unstable; often used to create drama or resolution.Interval: The distance between two notes. Common intervals include 2nd, 3rd, 5th and Octaves.Inversion: A chord where the root is not the lowest note. Changes the feel/sound of the chord.Key: The tonal center or home scale of a piece, which determines which chords are most commonly usedTriad: A basic three-note chord made of root, third and fifth. (D minor triad=D-F-A.)Voicing: Exploring different ways to arrange notes in chords can lead to fuller or more varied sound such as using inversions. Teaching Module19

contentSummary: A triad is a three-note chord built from a root, third and fifth. It is a group of three notes played or sung simultaneously. When we refer to the root, third and fifth, we mean that: zThe root is a base note (foundation note). zThe third is a third interval above the root. zThe fifth is a fifth note (a perfect 5th) above the root.
